title: Homes demolished without compensation on the North Buckingham canal in Nagapattinam
place: Nagapattinam district, Tamil Nadu, India, with resettlement sites at Okkiyum-Thuraipakkam and north Chennai

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Emergency Tsunami Reconstruction Project, project number P094513, credit IDA-40540, approved 3 May 2005 after the December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, effective 9 August 2005, closing extended from 30 April 2008 to 31 December 2011. US$235.0 million of the credit was cancelled because the closing date was not extended further. The completion report of 18 June 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Unsatisfactory against both the original and the revised objectives (ICR Review, 29 May 2013).

companies.name: Commissioner of Revenue Administration, Revenue Administration, Disaster Management and Mitigation Department, Government of Tamil Nadu
companies.role: Lead implementing agency named in the completion report, the state department that runs disaster relief and holds the district collectors under it. Thirteen implementing agencies carried out procurement; the Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board held the urban housing and the transit accommodation. No construction contractor is named for the canal works.

community: The completion report records that in Nagapattinam district, work to improve the North Buckingham canal ran ahead of the state's resettlement and rehabilitation policy: the local authorities demolished the affected structures without offering compensation and assistance. After the Bank's team learned of it, the Government of Tamil Nadu drew up retrofit measures and put them in place, and all six displaced families were offered cash grants for the impacts they had suffered. Five families had received the grant when the credit closed on 31 December 2011 and the state was still in the process of paying the sixth. At two resettlement sites built for tsunami-affected people, about 100 families of the existing host population were affected: at Okkiyum-Thuraipakkam all 29 host families were moved temporarily into nearby Slum Clearance Board housing to wait for permanent houses, and at the All India Radio site in north Chennai 60 of 70 families had shifted by the closing date, leaving 10 families in temporary shelter awaiting a permanent site. For the resettlement sites as a whole, 560 hectares of land was acquired, 330 hectares of it private land, bought by private negotiation under a special government order letting district collectors set compensation at up to 200 per cent of guideline or registered values; about 40 hectares was donated by local citizens. The completion report says state funds, not Bank funds, paid for that land. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the project team told it the project was in compliance with the resettlement policy at the time the completion report was written, and that the 100 families physically displaced in Tamil Nadu were either given alternative housing or were expected to be shortly; that is a statement by Bank staff, not a document.
outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2011 without a further extension, with one of the six Nagapattinam families still waiting for its grant and 10 host families at the north Chennai site still in temporary shelter. The completion report lists the difficulty of decommissioning and demolishing transit shelters, and unwillingness among beneficiaries to accept temporary relocation, among the lessons of in-situ urban resettlement.

title: House on Jomhori Boulevard expropriated for an Ahwaz sewerage pumping station
place: Jomhori Boulevard, Ahwaz, Khuzestan Province, Iran

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Ahwaz and Shiraz Water Supply and Sanitation Project, project number P071191, Loan 4738-IRN. The loan agreement of 17 July 2004 lends US$279,000,000 to the Islamic Republic of Iran (Loan Agreement, Section 2.01). The Board approved it on 25 May 2004, it became effective on 17 November 2004 and it closed on 30 September 2009 without extension; US$200.6 million was disbursed (Implementation Completion and Results Report, ICR00001441, 31 March 2010, data sheet). The project was environmental Category A, because of the water and wastewater treatment plants, sludge and effluent reuse, industrial effluent discharge and the archaeological sites in Shiraz; the completion report says OP 4.01 on Environmental Assessment was triggered, that OPN 11.03 on cultural property was also triggered for Shiraz, a policy the same report's safeguards compliance section instead calls OP 4.11, and that the project received an exemption from OP 7.50 (paragraph on soundness of background analysis, page 9). The appraisal document has a section on Involuntary Resettlement OP/BP 4.12 and concludes that the project complies with its requirements (Project Appraisal Document, 29 April 2004). The completion report rates the outcome Unsatisfactory, bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 September 2010 (report no. ICRR13381) also rates the outcome Unsatisfactory. Implementing agencies were the Ahwaz Water and Wastewater Company, the Shiraz Water and Wastewater Company and the National Water and Wastewater Engineering Company.

companies.name: Ahwaz Water and Wastewater Company
companies.role: The city-level water and sewerage utility that carried out the Ahwaz half of the project, alongside the National Water and Wastewater Engineering Company, the third implementing agency, which the completion report describes as sitting within the Ministry of Energy and reporting directly to the Vice Minister for Water Supply and Sanitation. A technical support unit in the utility carried out the project's procurement and held its environment and safety officer. No construction contractor is named in the documents for this pumping station.

community: The project built water and sewerage networks, treatment plants and pumping stations in Ahwaz and Shiraz. The completion report of 31 March 2010 gives one site where land was taken from people. For pumping station AS23-1 on Jomhori Boulevard in Ahwaz, a plot of 800 square metres, the land 'was a residential house that belonged to two individual owners and agreement with them was reached, a down payment was paid, and the property was expropriated'. The report then says: 'Since the deal involved resettlement of at least eight individuals, an abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) was prepared.' The report does not say whether the balance of the price was paid, where the eight went, or what they received beyond the price of the house. It says Land Acquisition Plans were prepared wherever land was expropriated and Resettlement Action Plans wherever resettlement of people or displacement of livelihoods was involved, and that several resettlement and land acquisition reviews were carried out during implementation. The same paragraph of the completion report says the environmental impact of the investments was generally positive and that there were no compliance issues in either Ahwaz or Shiraz. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 September 2010 says that, according to the completion report, there was adequate compliance with social safeguards policies and procedures in both cities. The appraisal document of 29 April 2004 had said of the expropriations it listed: 'In no case are residences or current economic activities or livelihoods affected.' What it listed for Ahwaz was an unused agricultural plot of 67 hectares from 13 local farmers, with compensation then being negotiated, and eight pumping-station plots of which two were privately owned, all of it described as undeveloped urban land; its Ahwaz annex adds 'There are no holders of other rights, no relocation or loss of shelter, income, or livelihoods.' The house on Jomhori Boulevard is in none of those entries and appears only in the 2010 report. The appraisal figure is 67 hectares in the document's text and 67.5 hectares in its own expropriation table. No outcome document found says what happened to those 13 owners. The completion report also records that land acquisition issues caused long delays to the works.
outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2009 with the project unfinished. The completion report says critical components, including treatment plants, pumping stations and pipes, were incomplete or under construction and not fully operational, that unaccounted-for water deteriorated in Ahwaz, and that the financial position of both water companies worsened. It says lack of completion 'will disproportionately affect the poorer segments of the society' because most of the remaining components sit in poor neighbourhoods. Where it makes the same point in the present tense, in the list of risks, it adds in the next sentence that the proportion of completed works is also higher in poorer neighbourhoods, given the project's focus on the poor. The Independent Evaluation Group's review puts it as lack of completion having 'disproportionately affected the poorer segments of society'. No later document was found on the house at Jomhori Boulevard or on the eight people.

title: Three worker deaths and the moving of 72 roadside shop owners on Iraq's Expressway 1
place: Expressway No. 1 between Nasiriya and Basra, Iraq, with the Girsheen-Suheila section of the North-South corridor in the north of the country

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Transport Corridors Project, project number P131550, loan IBRD-83220, US$355.0 million, approved 19 December 2013, effective 30 March 2015 after a twelve-month delay while a government was formed, closing extended from 31 December 2019 to 30 June 2023, US$337.6 million disbursed. The project was assigned environmental category A and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Disbursement for part of the loan, the activities under the Roads and Bridges Directorate, was suspended over delays in fully complying with the social safeguards policies, specifically over updating and implementing the resettlement plan to the Bank's satisfaction for the vendors along segments R7 and R8 (completion report of 18 December 2023, paragraph 73). The completion report rates the outcome Highly Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and quality of monitoring Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Satisfactory and quality of monitoring Substantial (ICR Review, 2 May 2024, section 11).

companies.name: State Commission for Roads and Bridges, Ministry of Construction, Housing, Municipalities and Public Works, Iraq
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report, which ran the works through project management teams at the Commission and at the Roads and Bridges Directorate. The completion report says the larger works contracts were awarded to international contractors but names none of them.

community: Three workers were killed on the project. The completion report gives the cause of each: the driver of a pick-up van who collided with a parked vehicle; a supervising engineer run over by a project vehicle during site supervision; and a daily worker hit by a pick-up car while standing on the road. The report says these incidents were completely avoidable had higher levels of worker awareness, training, safety provisions and close supervision been in place. Several traffic accidents happened during the rehabilitation of long sections of Expressway No. 1, both inside and outside the temporary traffic management zones; the report records no deaths among the public inside those zones, and says the Bank required the project team to report and document accidents at once, a practice that did not exist before, under threat of suspending disbursement. On segments R7 and R8, 72 shop owners immediately next to the right of way were resettled to dedicated serviced lay-bys, and those who had been trading informally were legalised. The completion report presents this as a gain: compensating squatters rather than only landlords was new in Iraq, the poorest traders benefited, and vendors were able to expand their premises at the new location, with better access and parking. The project was partly suspended for disbursement because the resettlement plan for these vendors was not updated and implemented to the Bank's satisfaction. On the new Girsheen-Suheila road corridor in the north, land had to be acquired, and the plan covered the amount of farmland taken, crop loss, who was eligible, the rates for crops and fixed assets, and extra help for three affected people below the poverty line. Delays in paying affected people were observed and the Bank reminded the roads directorate that no civil work could start on the ground before the compensation was paid. All compensation due was disbursed by May 2016.
outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2023. The completion report rates its outcome Highly Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group rates it Satisfactory. Average traffic deaths across the project road segments for 2020 to 2023 came to 23 a year against a baseline of 113 and a target of 87; the results table in the body of the same report gives 21 for that indicator where its text and its annex give 23. The report says the project obliged contractors to comply with occupational health and safety procedures and to provide workers with sanitary dormitories and paid rest time.

title: Houses and shops demolished for heritage and tourism works in five Jordanian towns
place: Jerash, Karak, Salt, Ajloun and Madaba, Jordan

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Third Tourism Development Project, Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Urban Development, project number P081823, loan IBRD-74260, US$56.0 million at approval on 30 January 2007, reduced to US$55.0 million, effective 16 August 2007, closing extended from 30 September 2012 to 31 March 2014, US$50.78 million disbursed. The project budget line for land acquisition, expropriation and resettlement was raised from US$5.86 million to US$7.60 million at the Level 1 restructuring of 14 July 2011, and the completion report's Annex 1 carries US$7.60 million as the actual or latest estimate against the US$5.86 million appraisal estimate. The completion report of 30 January 2015 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group also rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and rates risk to development outcome Significant (ICR Review, 9 June 2015).

companies.name: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Jordan
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report. Its Technical Development Department ran the project unit; the appraisal document planned to recruit 17 extra staff for it. The completion report rates the department's performance Moderately Satisfactory, mainly on poor monitoring. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

community: The works ran through densely built town centres and took land and buildings. The completion report says the actual resettlement impacts were slightly smaller than the impacts documented in the resettlement action plans at appraisal, and its own table gives what was actually done against what was planned. Permanent land acquisition came to 12,408 square metres against 20,332 planned. Residential houses were demolished over 2,905 square metres against 4,107 planned, 2,505 of it in Karak and 400 in Jerash. Commercial stores were demolished over 1,750 square metres against 7,136 planned, 1,555 of it in Jerash and 195 in Ajloun. Forty-six households were affected against 52 planned: 6 in Jerash, 11 in Karak, 17 in Salt and 12 in Ajloun. Madaba had none. In Ajloun, vendors had to be relocated before the works could start, and the report says that and land acquisition in Salt were where the process took longest. The actual resettlement cost was higher than planned, 4.96 million Jordanian dinars against 4.18 million, about US$7 million against US$5.9 million, because the compensation actually paid was higher than planned. The completion report says compensation rates for all lost assets were set on market value and reflected replacement cost, that community liaison officers in each city acted between the municipalities and affected people, that all affected people were satisfied with the compensation and resettlement package, and that renters eventually returned to improved and renovated shops.
outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2014. The documents record no outstanding compensation and no unresolved grievance. The Independent Evaluation Group notes that the main text of the completion report does not discuss compliance with the policy on cultural property, and that the borrower's own comments record a few minor issues found during construction and corrected.

title: Households and market vendors moved for heritage works in Tripoli, Tyre and Saida
place: Khan el Askar and the old souks, Tripoli, with the covered markets of Tyre and Saida, Lebanon

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Additional Financing for the Cultural Heritage and Urban Development Project, project number P116197, loan IBRD-81370, US$27.0 million, approved 12 April 2012, with effectiveness delayed by a hung parliament. It topped up the original project, number P050529, loan IBRD-71660, US$31.5 million, approved 17 April 2003. One completion report covers both, dated 15 June 2017, and the operation closed on 31 December 2016. The additional loan paid for the later batches of the same works in the same five cities, Baalbeck, Byblos, Saida, Tripoli and Tyre. Its Bank financing was allocated US$17.9 million to rehabilitation of historic city centres and urban infrastructure, US$6.7 million to archaeological sites and US$2.2 million to institutional strengthening (completion report, Annex 1, project financing by component, additional financing). The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory and safeguards Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, assessing efficiency as modest because of high cost overruns (ICR Review, 22 November 2017). The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group also published a field-based Project Performance Assessment Report on 13 August 2019.

companies.name: Council for Development and Reconstruction of the Republic of Lebanon
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report. A public body reporting to the Lebanese Council of Ministers that contracts and supervises state infrastructure works; two staff of the Directorate General of Antiquities worked full time on its premises to handle archaeological finds. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

community: The works involved involuntary resettlement affecting 760 project-affected people across Tripoli, Tyre and Saida. Six resettlement action plans were prepared. The completion report's own table records what happened: 38 households with 209 people physically relocated from Khan el Askar blocks A and B in Tripoli; 33 households with 124 people physically relocated from Khan el Askar block C; 280 vendors recorded as physically relocated into the new marketplace in Tripoli, the same figure a 2011 project document had already used for the vendors the revised Tripoli plan covered; 3 tenants temporarily relocated from the Salameh building in Saida; and 144 vendors temporarily relocated for the new marketplace in Tyre. A sixth plan, for the physical relocation of 31 people from small shops and warehouses at Khan el-Askar, was never implemented because that component was cancelled. The Tripoli marketplace works were halted for four years from 2012 by active shooting in the city, the census of affected people had to be redone, and that plan was finished three months after the project closed. The Bank's field assessment, published in 2019, found that in the rebuilt covered market in Tyre the expected gains had not arrived: on the day of the visit the market was deserted and the vegetable and fruit sellers were playing cards for want of customers. Interviews recorded fewer permanent vendors working in the market than the resettlement plan had arranged for, fruit and vegetable sellers undercut by traders outside the market who pay no fees, and parking cut to 36 spaces where vendors had been told there would be 180. The market association collected the signatures of hundreds of vendors opposed to the changes and organised two sit-ins. In Tripoli, residents of the historic souk houses told the assessment team they had not been contacted before or during the works and had gone to the engineers on site themselves. Shop owners and tenants in the old souks said they were consulted and promised their objections would be considered, and felt that did not happen. Against this, the completion report says all six plans were financed by the project, four were satisfactorily implemented by closing, the Tripoli plan was satisfactorily implemented by the time of the report, and the new Tripoli marketplace won the Bank's 2017 Sustainable Development Vice-Presidency award.
outcome: The operation closed on 31 December 2016 and the Tripoli marketplace resettlement finished three months later. The Bank's own field assessment of 2019 found the Tyre market underused and traditional businesses around the new public square losing trade, with owners saying the area was being turned over to tourism.

title: A Dennery Family's Land Was Built On Without Consent and Only Their Coconut Trees Were Paid For
place: The north embankment of the Dennery River, Dennery Village, Saint Lucia

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD and IDA)
lenders.role: The land acquisition and involuntary resettlement report of 20 February 2007 is headed "LC Disaster Management Project II" and is filed in the World Bank's archive under Additional Financing to the Second St. Lucia Disaster Management Project (P111708), whose approval ICIJ's table records as 15 July 2008. The report says the land acquisition request comes from Component 1 of the project, "Physical Prevention and Mitigation Works", which includes the coastal and flood protection works for Dennery Village, and that the request for additional financing to extend the north embankment "triggers the Bank's Operational Policy 4.12, regarding involuntary resettlement". It says the extension requires 6,039 square metres to be acquired out of total lands of 19,895.77 square metres, that this land is privately owned, and that the government now needs to acquire 30 per cent of the lands so the contractor can proceed. The works that had already been built are the parent project's. A Government of Saint Lucia press release of 7 February 2005 says the government secured 7.5 million dollars from two World Bank agencies for the coastal and flood protection of Dennery Village under the Second St. Lucia Disaster Mitigation Project: an IBRD loan of 3.7 million dollars and an IDA credit of 3.8 million dollars, with bids invited under World Bank guidelines. No completion report and no evaluation review filed under the additional financing number could be reached, and no document found for it states a loan or credit number or an amount.

companies.name: Mirai Construction Company Limited
companies.role: The contractor for the Dennery Coastal Protection Phases 1 and 2, awarded at a contract price of 6,683,042.53 East Caribbean dollars. The report says those works began on 26 July 2005 and were completed in the first week of September 2006, and comprised a 415-metre buried revetment, offshore breakwaters, an armoured berm and landfill. The report also names a second contract, the Dennery River Trou a Leau Ravine Works, awarded to Hippolyte Equipment Services (HES) and completed on 30 July 2007. It does not say which of the two contracts built the length of embankment that crossed the family's land.

companies.name: Smith Warner International
companies.role: The consulting engineers, of Jamaica, who prepared the final design report of October 2003, whose contract was varied in February 2006 so they could carry out a topographical survey of the area, and who supervised the earlier works contract. The report says the portion of the design that needed the family's land was left out of the bill of quantities because of land acquisition issues, and that the ministry considered in hindsight that time would have been saved by better communication at that stage.

community:
On 17 February 2007 a World Bank safeguards specialist met three representatives of the property owners whose land was needed to extend the north embankment of the Dennery River. Seven subdivided plots were represented. The report of that meeting, dated 20 February 2007, records what the owners said about what had already been done to their land.

The owners said their land had been used without their consent or any consultation for transporting, storing and dumping materials, and that their trees had been cut down. One loss is larger than that: "an area belonging to the Biscette - Regis family was used for the construction of the existing embankment without consent or compensation; the only compensation paid was for some coconuts trees that were removed." The family's representative, who speaks for four subdivided plots straddling the land where the embankment already stands and the land still to be acquired, said they were never informed or consulted about the project's designs, and had understood that the embankment would run along the river's edge. The report says the participants also spoke of their sense of helplessness, there being no grievance mechanism and nobody responsible they could take their concerns to. Their first contact with the project's intention to build an embankment, the report says, "was when the trucks and heavy construction equipment passed through or near their property".

The report records a meeting held at the end of January 2007 at which, it says, the contractor explained what his company would do and "stated that the government would expropriate the necessary land with or without their consent".

The same owners are for the works. The report says the participants agreed that the project itself will benefit their properties and the well-being of their town, that they acknowledge the benefits and "are eager to see the works extended and completed as far in advance as possible before this year's June storms", and that they had suggestions drawn from living through Hurricane Debbie and other floods, among them more drains and regular clearing of the existing one, which keeps getting clogged with elephant grass.

The report says the land still to be taken is 6,039 of 19,895.77 square metres for a 180-metre extension, that the original designs of the north embankment were over 90 per cent complete, and that since the designs were drawn in 2002 the owners had put up fences and enclosures on the land to be regraded.
outcome: No completion report, evaluation review or later plan filed under the additional financing number could be reached, so no document found says whether the Biscette-Regis family was ever paid for the land the existing embankment stands on, whether the 6,039 square metres were acquired, or whether the 180-metre extension was built. The report of 20 February 2007 says a notice of the land to be affected had been sent for publication and that a valuation of each acquired property would follow a survey, with a tribunal process available for concerns and claims.

title: Farmland taken and two households moved for Lesotho's road works
place: Nyenye to Makhoroana road, Leribe District, Lesotho

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Lesotho Integrated Transport Project (P075566), Credit IDA-42370 approved 19 October 2006, with later IDA-48270, grants IDA H-2550 and IDA H-6230 and trust fund TF-90728; the Financing Agreement for Credit 4827-LS and Grant H623-LS is dated 9 October 2010. The completion report of 21 December 2015 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 June 2016 both rate the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The review rates the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory. The completion report rates safeguards performance moderately unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Ministry of Public Works and Transport, Lesotho
companies.role: Ran the project through a project implementation unit with posts for an environment and social coordinator, a resettlement desk and an HIV/AIDS coordinator. Both of the unit's safeguards specialists left in the project's second year and were not replaced for the additional financing, and no safeguards specialist joined the lender's own supervision missions for that stage.

community: The credit paid for road works in Lesotho, including two bridges over the Senqu and Senqunyane rivers and work on two junction roads, Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng and Nyenye to Makhoroana. Floods in March 2011 damaged both roads so badly that the planned resealing had to become full rehabilitation; there was not enough credit for all 64 km, so the lender paid for the first 20 km of the Nyenye to Makhoroana road and the government undertook to cover the remaining 17 km and the Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng road. The completion report says the first assessment found resettlement "confined to two households", but that compensation also had to be paid for many strips of farmland where the road was widened for bus and taxi stops. When the additional financing was added, the report says, the assessment of its safeguards impacts was underestimated and implementation was unsatisfactory: environmental measures were neither systematically monitored nor documented, workers' safety measures "were only respected partially", and further resettlement activities were found later. New culverts, added when the road design changed, "induced adverse impacts on farmland", and the mission that wrote the report saw stones and loose material fallen onto the roads in many places. A small number of temporary market stalls were moved to make room for the works at Makhoroana. A new taxi rank was being built on land the local chief gave, and the report's authors objected that the taxi association had still not been formally engaged. No resettlement completion report was prepared. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats these findings and says that "it is not clear from the ICR whether the resettlement activities were complete at project closure". The report also records that prostitutes went to the construction camp, that condoms were often not available there because of its remote location, and that a social impacts study at completion found HIV infection rates had risen; the implementing agency denies that less attention was given to this under the additional financing.
outcome: The project closed in 2015. The completion report rates safeguards performance moderately unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group says the report's account of safeguards compliance is unclear and that it cannot be told from it whether the project complied at closing. No resettlement completion report was produced, so there is no record of what the affected farmers were finally paid.

title: Motorway built on land whose owners had not been paid
place: Tabanovce to Kumanovo, Corridor X, North Macedonia

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Second Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, P091723, loan IBRD-48590. Approved 29 May 2007, closed 30 June 2012 after a nine-month extension of an original closing date of 30 September 2011. Loan of 15 million euros, equivalent to US$20 million; the completion report's data sheet gives US$20.52 million disbursed, while the Independent Evaluation Group's review gives US$20.27 million in its loan column. Environmental category B. In March 2009 the Bank's team found that compensation for the road upgrade had not been paid to all landowners before the contractor started work, and the Bank sent a Warning of Suspension of Disbursement for the part of the loan covering the road upgrade. The completion report of 12 December 2012 rates the outcome Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 September 2013, which rates overall Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory against the report's Satisfactory.

companies.name: Agency for State Roads
companies.role: The national road agency and the implementing body for the road upgrade, including land acquisition and compensation payments; its Director was the project coordinator. The revised resettlement plan required it to hold the full assessed compensation in a special account. The completion report names no construction contractor, referring only to "the contractor".

companies.name: Customs Administration
companies.role: A unit of the Ministry of Finance, and the implementing body for the Blace border crossing component, where 27 parcels of land had to be acquired that the government had told the Bank would not be needed.

community: Land was taken for the 7.3 km upgrade of the Tabanovce to Kumanovo section of Corridor X to motorway standard. The completion report of 12 December 2012 records "about 102 affected owners involving about 294 parcels of land". In March 2009 the Bank's team found that compensation for that land "was not paid to all landowners prior to start of works by the contractor", contrary to the Resettlement Action Plan and the loan agreement, because some owners had gone to court to raise the amounts. The report calls the delays in payment "a serious safeguard violation which were corrected in time and detracted slightly from the very positive outcome". The Bank sent a Warning of Suspension of Disbursement for the road part of the loan. The warning was lifted a few months later when the Bank and the government agreed to amend the plan and the loan agreement so that works could proceed as long as money for compensation was set aside in the road agency's budget; the national law was changed in the same direction. Four or five court cases were still open when the project closed; the report says they have since been decided, and that under Macedonian law payment from the state budget follows automatically once a court makes an award. At the Blace crossing to Kosovo, the government assured the Bank during preparation that no land acquisition was needed; at implementation 27 parcels had to be acquired, and the completion report says this held up the start of civil works for more than two years. The report says 102 households were expected to lose part of their land holdings and that no residence was affected; the resettlement plan of 5 April 2007 says there would be no physical displacement of persons and no buildings to demolish.
outcome: The motorway is open and the completion report says all land acquisition cases have been resolved. The safeguard violation is recorded in both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review; the review says it was "quickly" addressed. title: Herders off the East Tsankhi coalfield: two households part-compensated, 17 given nothing
place: East Tsankhi coalfield, Ulaan nuur valley, Tsogttsetsii soum, Umnugobi (Omnogovi) province, Mongolia

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P108768, Mining Sector Institutional Strengthening Technical Assistance Project, credit IDA-44890 (C4489-MN) and grant IDA-H4110 (H411-MN), together SDR 5.72 million, the equivalent of US$9.3 million; the financing agreement was conformed on 7 October 2008. The completion report of 30 March 2017 gives approval on 26 June 2008, effectiveness on 4 May 2009, a mid-term review on 1 November 2011, an original closing date of 31 December 2012 and actual closing on 31 December 2015, with restructurings on 2 July 2012, 10 January 2014 and 30 March 2015; SDR 5.66 million was disbursed. Environmental category B. No safeguard policy was triggered at appraisal. The report says that "following conduct of a safeguards review of the project in 2013, OP/BP 4.12 (Involuntary Resettlement) was triggered retroactively as part of the Restructuring in January 2014. This was in respect of the earlier financing by MSISTAP of the pre-feasibility study for ETT's East Tsankhi coal mine. The relocation of two winter shelters had taken place in 2010 in connection with development of this mine and more resettlements were anticipated to take place as ETT's coal mining operations expanded (albeit notrelated to MSISTAP or the East Tsankhi pre-feasibility study)." The two documents do not say the same thing about cause. The report puts the relocation “in connection with development of this mine”. The Evaluation Group’s review of the report makes the study itself the cause: the policy “was triggered as a result of the relocation of two winter shelters by an activity financed by the project”, and in its supervision section, “Two winter shelters had to be relocated because of a pre-feasibility study financed by the project.” The project then paid for the remedial resettlement action plan and the resettlement policy framework for the mine's operator. The report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, risk to the development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review, filed under 22 December 2017 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome and risk, rates borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and keeps Bank performance at Moderately Satisfactory while saying the report's own rating "should have been Moderately Unsatisfactory" under the harmonised rules.

companies.name: Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi JSC
companies.role: State-owned operator of the East Tsankhi coalfield and a subsidiary of the state holding company Erdenes MGL, whose pre-feasibility study for the mine the Bank's credit paid for. The remedial plan says it had no unit responsible for resettlement, that "ETT is just beginning to address resettlement with very weak capacity", and that it "has focused mostly on the extraction and transportation of coal and ignoring key requirements for adequate resettlement such as cut-off date."

companies.name: Ministry of Finance of Mongolia
companies.role: Implementing agency for the credit, through the project implementation unit it housed; the steering committee was chaired by its State Secretary.

community: The Bank's technical assistance credit paid for a pre-feasibility study of the East Tsankhi coal mine, and the Bank later decided that this made the resettlement at the mine its business. The remedial resettlement action plan it then financed, drafted in December 2014 by a Mongolian research centre and an Australian consultancy, says the mine area "was the herders' important pasture resource prior to the commencement of East Tsankhi mining operation in 2010." It counts 26 households hit by the mine: "A total of 26 households were impacted by displacement due to ETT company's Eastern Tsankhi mining operation, out of which 2 households received incomplete compensation for physical displacement, however, 17 households impacted by economic displacement have not received any compensation." Two households were moved by the operator and two by a different coal company, and five more were moved by that other company inside a five-kilometre belt; the plan counts nine households physically displaced in all and 17 economically displaced. Of the two the operator moved, both are named. One lost two winter camps, each with its own hand-dug well, and about 1,250 hectares of seasonal pasture; he was given two winter camps by the soum government, 15 million tugrug from the operator and jobs for three of his children, and asked for a well at the new camp; the plan says "The winter camp provided by the company did not have a water well, which makes the winter camp to be impossible to use; thus Erdenebileg's opportunity for herding the livestock for livelihood was limited and he now lives in the soum center." It adds that no inventory of his assets or income was taken at the time, so "whether 15 million tugrugs are adequate to compensate the loss occured has not been properly studied or estimated." The second lost a winter camp, a deep well, about 550 hectares of seasonal pasture, a hot-water facility and a hectare of planted land; he was given 30 million tugrug, a new deep well, a winter camp from the other company and 0.7 hectares from the soum government "after running around for a while". He told the drafters: "The company drilled the deep-water well, but there was no waterbed (old water well provided 5 tons of water per 15 minutes, but new well works for 20 minutes until it dewaters and we need to wait another 3 hours until to regenerate the water). After the displacement, nobody visited us; when we asked about the hot water facility, they responded that the request was submitted to the management, and already 2 years passed." The 17 households who lost summer and autumn grazing were left out of the operator’s resettlement work altogether, and the plan’s table names all 17, two inside the mining licence area and 15 in the five-kilometre zone, with the pasture each lost running from 65 hectares to 2,772 hectares. Against 14 of the names it records “Out-migrated”, against one “Deceased”, and against one that he lost his livestock and settled in a bag centre; the seventeenth name carries no status and her pasture is counted in the same cell as another household’s 2,538 hectares. One of them is quoted: "Before ETT started its mining operation, we used to stay throughout the summer and fall in the southeast of Ulaan Toirom. Since the mining operation started, it became impossible to stay the same area and we moved to Tsagaan Ovoo Bagh." The plan says the exclusion happened because only herders with fixed assets such as winter camps and wells were counted, no cut-off date was ever announced, and the summer and autumn pasture that fattens the animals was treated as nothing. Its evaluation section says: "The company chose one package of compensation and mainly forced the package to the affected persons, therefore affected persons' right to freely choose from various options was limited"; "Committed compensation package was not fully provided, implementation of the compensation was not monitored, and the livelihood support measures were not planned and implemented"; "The post displacement livelihood of the affected persons was not monitored and evaluated. The strategy was to provide the compensation and forget about the affected persons"; and that there is no grievance mechanism. It also notes that the coal haul road to the Chinese border was not considered at all, and that the households of Tsagaan-Ovoo Bagh, a former mine workers’ village, would be affected by dust once the operator piled its tailings nearby from 2015 — a forecast, not a finding, and one the plan sizes twice, at 137 households in its impacts section and “over 100” in its evaluation.
outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2015. The remedial resettlement action plan and the resettlement policy framework were prepared and disclosed, both still marked draft, and the Bank treated the amended safeguards covenant as complied with on that basis. No document found says whether the 17 uncompensated households were ever paid, whether the hot-water facility was built, or whether the unusable winter camp was given a well. A cumulative impact assessment for the area, financed by a different Bank credit, was still unfinished when this one closed.

title: Five deaths and a failed compensation process on Mozambique's urban climate works
place: Beira, Sofala Province, and the ravines 3 and 4 site in Maputo, Mozambique

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Cities and Climate Change Project (P123201), Credit IDA-50660, US$120 million approved 3 April 2012; the Financing Agreement for Credit 5066-MZ is dated 2012, the day on its signature line being illegible in the disclosed text. The credit is SDR 78.2 million, US$120 million equivalent. Additional financing of US$15.75 million from the Strategic Climate Fund under the Pilot Program for Climate Resilience, made up of a US$6.5 million loan and a US$9.25 million grant, was approved by the Board on 23 October 2014 and declared effective on 7 April 2015. Actual disbursement US$122,517,360.69 in credit and US$15,561,840.66 in grants. Closed 30 September 2020, against an original closing date of 15 December 2017. The completion report of 30 March 2021 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 August 2021 both rate the outcome Satisfactory.

lenders.name: KfW (German Development Bank)
lenders.role: Parallel financing of EUR 18 million for the green urban infrastructure works on the Chiveve River in downtown Beira, alongside the Bank's additional financing. Those works ran past the Bank project's closing date, and the safeguards left unfinished at closing, including the return of market vendors, were handled under a post-closing plan the Bank monitored with KfW.

companies.name: Administracao de Infra-estruturas de Agua e Saneamento (AIAS)
companies.role: Mozambique's water and sanitation infrastructure administration, under the Ministry of Public Works, Housing and Water Resources. The project implementation unit for the drainage and green infrastructure works in Beira and Maputo sat inside it, and it was the body the Bank held to the resettlement and labour audits after closing.

community: The project paid for drainage works in Beira and Maputo and for green urban infrastructure along the Chiveve River in central Beira. The completion report says the works in Beira "recorded recurrent issues of non-compliance with OHS and community health and safety plans" and names the deaths. For the Beira drainage works it counts "the fatality of one worker and three community members", and its footnote gives the causes: a worker hit by a third-party vehicle while moving between work sites; a nine-year-old child who drowned in the retention basin construction site outside working hours; and two people killed in traffic accidents involving the contractor's vehicles. For the green infrastructure works in Beira a second footnote records "a fatality of a 7-year old child who was hit by a contractor's vehicle". Those works' main difficulty, the report says, was the contractor's lack of commitment to community and worker safety and to national employment and labour law, including weekly rest and limits on working hours. The report also names two more deaths it does not attribute to the project: another child found dead in the drainage canals outside the construction sites, and a body found in the Chiveve retention basin during construction. In Beira the project built 21 new houses and 81 latrines for structures the works hit, paid for 498 trees, and compensated 610 people who grew vegetables in small plots known locally as machambas, reaching 98 per cent of them for their crops. In Maputo the report says resettlement "was problematic". The canal's original line would have affected seven houses at a site known as ravines 3 and 4. By the time the plan was being written the number of affected people had risen to 18, and they had already left the land after being paid by a private developer who was buying the land rights from the Municipality of Maputo. The Bank's team could not get clear information from the agency or the municipality and demanded an independent audit. The audit found the money the developer paid "did not meet the requirements of Bank safeguard policies and was not developed in accordance with the applicable Mozambican legislation". It told the project to give a new plot to one affected person who had wanted to be compensated by the municipality instead, to provide land papers to the others, to help those who had lost their source of income, and to pay six months of lost income. The audit was presented in February 2018 and the project reported the fixes done in June 2018, before the works started.
outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2020, almost three years late. The safeguards rating on the municipal grant component fell to Moderately Unsatisfactory in 2016, after a review found that 20 municipalities lacked the capacity to run environmental and social measures on small works, and was back at Moderately Satisfactory by closing. A labour audit finished in October 2020 and an environmental audit in November 2020; by mid-March 2021 the contractor had not produced satisfactory evidence for 11 of the labour audit's corrective actions, 15 per cent of them, and 14 of the environmental audit's measures, 21 per cent, were late. The updated plan for putting market vendors back into the new Chiveve market had been sent to the Bank but could only be carried out after the works were handed to the agency and the municipality in late March or early April 2021, a handover delayed by Cyclone Eloise. The green infrastructure works also had direct impacts on protected mangroves in the Chiveve basin, and restoring them was part of the post-closing plan.

title: Right-of-way clearance, 13,600 job losses and a mine death on the Sena railway
place: Sena railway line, Dondo to Moatize, Mozambique

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Beira Railway Project (P082618), Credit 3991-MOZ, US$110 million, approved 14 October 2004, Development Credit Agreement and project agreements with the concession company and the state ports and railways enterprise all dated 16 December 2004. The completion report of 27 June 2012 rates the outcome Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Unsatisfactory; it gives the risk to the development outcome as Significant in its risk assessment section and as Substantial in its summary data sheet, and the two are not reconciled. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 6 November 2013 rates the outcome Unsatisfactory, the risk High and both Bank and borrower performance Unsatisfactory, where the completion report rated borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Companhia dos Caminhos de Ferro da Beira (CCFB)
companies.role: The concession company that held the Beira railway system. The appraisal document records its shares split 51 per cent to the concessionaire consortium and 49 per cent to the state railway and ports enterprise, which the completion report says left the public side with little or no leverage over major decisions.

companies.name: RITES Limited
companies.role: Indian state railway consultancy. With Ircon International it formed the consortium awarded the Beira railway concession on 30 August 2004 after international competitive bidding, holding 51 per cent of the concession company; the two also set up the joint venture RICON to manage the project. Railway Gazette reported in February 2007 that the pair were rebuilding the line under a US$175 million concession awarded in 2004.

companies.name: Ircon International Limited
companies.role: Indian state railway construction company, the other half of the concessionaire consortium holding 51 per cent of the concession company and a partner in the RICON joint venture that managed the works.

companies.name: Portos e Caminhos de Ferro de Mocambique, E.P. (CFM)
companies.role: Mozambique's state ports and railways enterprise, which held 49 per cent of the concession company while also supervising the project for the government. The completion report says this blurred whether it was regulator, policy maker, client or operator, and that its 49 per cent stake biased its supervision. It carried out the resettlement and the environmental clean-up, and it and the independent engineer intervened several times on safety, as far as expelling managers, stopping work and closing workers' camps.

community: The credit paid for rebuilding the Sena railway line between Dondo and Moatize, closed since 1983 and booby-trapped with landmines during the war. The completion report puts the rehabilitation component at 600 km and describes the line de-mined as 671 km. The line had to be cleared of mines, within 15 metres each side, before work could start; clearance of the whole line finished in October 2006, and de-mining teams went back out whenever contractors found residual mines. The completion report says: "Sadly, one worker was killed by these residual mines. Five more were killed in rail accidents." On people moved, the report records that "Thirty-seven households, five businesses and five religious facilities were relocated to make way for a 50m right of way on each side of the line", and that all the individuals and businesses were compensated. It also records that 13,600 staff, all of them employees of the state ports and railways enterprise, were retrenched as a precondition of the concession, that they were retrained, and that around 6,000 found work in new trades. On safety the report says occupational health and safety compliance "had not been addressed", that "Health and Safety at work standards at all sites were extremely low and the work conditions were often hazardous", and that construction waste and unrestored borrow pits were still outstanding at the final mission in December 2011. It says there was a visible and documented lack of concern for health and safety by the consortium, that the state enterprise and the independent engineer intervened several times, to the point of expelling managers, stopping work and closing workers' camps, and that those records could have been the base for more stringent action by the Bank, or for forcing cancellation of contracts with contravening contractors, but that this was never done; the Independent Evaluation Group repeats the passage. Both documents say compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy was reported as satisfactory or highly satisfactory throughout.
outcome: The concession was terminated at the end of 2011 and the government took the rail system back. The completion report rates the project Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group also rates Bank performance Unsatisfactory, saying design and supervision both fell short. Of the 13,600 retrenched staff, the report says around 6,000 found work in new trades; it gives no figure for the rest. Railway Gazette reported in February 2007 that services on the southern section were to resume before March that year, with the concessionaires hoping to finish the whole 670 km network by May 2009.

title: Crops destroyed with no compensation paid in a Mauritanian irrigation perimeter, and two seasons of crops lost in Mali
place: An unnamed irrigation perimeter in the Senegal River valley, Mauritania

lenders.name: World Bank (International Development Association)
lenders.role: Project P093826, Senegal River Basin Multi-purpose Water Resources Development Project, first phase of an adaptable programme. IDA Credit 41820 to Mali, SDR 21.0 million (about US$30.08 million equivalent); IDA Credit 41830 to Mauritania, SDR 22.2 million (about US$31.78 million); IDA Credit 41840 to Senegal, SDR 21.0 million (about US$30.08 million); IDA Grant H2310 to Guinea, SDR 12.60 million (about US$18.04 million); and Dutch Trust Fund grant TF-94727, SDR 8.5 million (about US$12.12 million). Original commitment SDR 76.80 million, of which SDR 68.01 million was disbursed. Approved 8 June 2006, effective 14 March 2007, restructured 17 June 2011, closing date extended from 8 September 2011 to 31 March 2013 (completion report ICR2653, 25 September 2013). Environmental category A. The completion report lists ten safeguard policies as triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP/GP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.04), Pest Management (OP 4.09), Cultural Property (OP 4.11), Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10), Forests (OP/BP 4.36), Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37), Projects in Disputed Areas (OP/BP/GP 7.60) and Projects on International Waterways (OP/BP/GP 7.50). The appraisal document's own table of policies triggered marks two of those ten in the No column, Indigenous Peoples (then OD 4.20, being revised as OP 4.10) and Projects in Disputed Areas (OP/BP/GP 7.60); no document reconciles that with the completion report's list of ten. The report rates the outcome Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, and Bank and borrower performance Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review of 30 June 2015 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory, and the quality of the completion report Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Organisation pour la Mise en Valeur du fleuve Sénégal (OMVS)
companies.role: The river basin organisation of Guinea, Mali, Mauritania and Senegal, and the project's implementing agency. Its project unit held the safeguards specialist and supervised the national executing agencies. Its own completion assessors recorded the destroyed crops in Mauritania.

companies.name: Société Nationale pour le Développement Rural (SONADER), Mauritania
companies.role: The national rural development company, the executing agency for the hydro-agricultural works in Mauritania. The completion report records procurement delays at SONADER for want of a procurement specialist.

community: The credits paid for water intakes, pumping stations, canals and the rehabilitation of irrigated land in the Senegal River basin: more than 4,400 hectares rehabilitated or newly developed, 88 kilometres of canals and 47 pumping stations. The completion report says safeguards work in the field often went to environmental questions at the expense of social ones, and that some issues were not tracked effectively: "For example in one perimeter in Mauritania the OMVS completion assessors noted that crops had been destroyed by the implementation of the project and no compensation had been paid." The same paragraph says contractors needed regular follow-up to keep up basic measures such as sanitation for labourers, that executing agencies met their responsibilities in most cases, and that local people spoke well of some mitigation measures, including walkways that cut the time and cost of reaching markets. In Mali, delays in rehabilitating agricultural land cost farmers their crops over two seasons, and the national executing agency distributed food directly to them. The basin organisation's own report, printed as an annex to the completion report under the activities the credits financed, repeats both findings, writing that it was the winter crops that were destroyed, and adds that there were no land disputes after the irrigation areas were rehabilitated. The report does not say how many people lost crops in either country.
outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2013. The completion report records the destroyed crops as uncompensated and does not say whether anything was paid afterwards. The Evaluation Group's review does not mention the destroyed crops, and says that despite the project being category A the completion report gives no clear statement of safeguard compliance.

title: Businesses and Fishermen Displaced at the Kamuzu Barrage

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Shire River Basin Management Program Phase I (P117617), Credit IDA-51250 of SDR 60.6 million (US$93.75 million equivalent) and Grant IDA-H7750 of SDR 20.2 million (US$31.25 million), approved 14 June 2012, effective 7 September 2012, closed 31 January 2019; US$121.88 million was disbursed against an appraisal cost of US$142.88 million, revised to US$131.58 million. The largest investment was the upgrading of the Kamuzu Barrage. The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Substantial (3 June 2019).

lenders.name: Global Environment Facility and Least Developed Countries Fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-12920 of US$5.078 million from the GEF Trust Fund and grant TF-12921 of US$1.5 million from the Least Developed Countries Fund, filed under P127866, both fully disbursed

companies.name: Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Water Development
companies.role: Carried out the project through its project management unit, which ran the resettlement plan with district authorities and contractors

community: The project rebuilt the Kamuzu Barrage on the Shire River at Liwonde. The completion report says the project's sub-projects did not entail physical relocation, and then records "economic displacement of 22 individual PAPs, 4 institutions (ESCOM, Maritime Police Office, Liwonde Town Council and Liwonde National Park) and 32 Fishermen at both the barrage and SRBA building". The resettlement plan of February 2014 names the people and lists what each stood to lose. One owner faced the complete closure of a camp business on the river, with a boat safari, a bar, restaurants, five guest rooms and twenty campsites. Another faced the replacement of a reception building, a bar, a house, a gate house and an old restaurant, and the loss of business income during construction. A third stood to lose the use of six shops and a dwelling house while the work went on. Eight people are listed, each losing a meat-selling business; the plan lists them as tenants of the town council's shelter and counts them elsewhere as eight households. A bicycle shed, a chip shed and a meat-roasting shed are each listed. Liwonde Town Assembly was to lose the income from six business shelters for three years, and two others the use of bare land, 0.25 and 0.35 hectares, for the three years of construction. The plan records that all of them said they were willing to give up their land provided they were properly compensated, and that they pressed to know when work would start so they could reposition themselves; the valuation team could not tell them. The project's flood-protection structures used voluntary land donation rather than purchase. A grievance system was set up and used, but the completion report says it was "gauged as partially non-inclusive to all PAPs because larger business owners did not use it", and that by project closure one grievance was still unresolved and in the courts. Elsewhere the same report says "all grievances were amicably resolved except one grievance by a lodge owner which is currently in court". The appraisal document also records that the barrage would lower dry-season water levels upstream in Liwonde National Park, reducing sandbars and floodplain grassland, and that the project area included restrictions on access to grazing in protected catchments.
outcome: The barrage was finished and the project closed on 31 January 2019 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. One grievance, by a lodge owner, was still in the courts at closing and no document records how it ended. In January 2026 the Malawi Freedom Network reported that lodge owners on the Lake Malawi shore in Mangochi and Salima had sued the National Water Resources Authority and the state generator EGENCO, accusing them of negligence in managing the barrage at Liwonde and saying that this caused flooding along the lake shore. That claim concerns the running of the barrage after the project closed, and it is an allegation in a case that has not been decided.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Nepal-India Regional Trade and Transport Project, project number P144335, credit IDA-52730 and grant IDA-H8630, approved 28 June 2013, effective 10 September 2013, closed 30 November 2021 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 June 2022). The project financed the Kathmandu inland container depot at Chobhar. The Bank told the Inspection Panel on 15 May 2020 that disbursements for the dry port had been withheld until February 2020 to address grievances and were then authorised because the grievances had been resolved (Inspection Panel Notice of Registration, 27 May 2020, paragraph 18). The project was restructured in December 2019 to extend the closing date by 23 months.

companies.name: Nepal Intermodal Transport Development Board
companies.role: The state body that built the dry port, under Nepal's Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, which the completion report names as an implementing agency. It ran the grievance notices the requesters answered.

companies.name: Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, Government of Nepal
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report for the trade component, which included the Kathmandu depot.

community: The depot was built on land at Chobhar, in Kirtipur Municipality south of Kathmandu, that the state had acquired decades earlier for the Himal Cement Factory, closed in 2002. Residents, mainly indigenous Newars, said the land should go back to its original owners and that disputes over that old acquisition were never settled. The Kathmandu Post reported on 18 January 2019 that the government said it had acquired 1,054 ropanis from the former factory, 228 ropanis of it for the dry port and 826 for an international exhibition centre, and quoted Panchha Lal Maharjan of the Chobhar Conservation Committee saying the government had not acquired all the private land, had not paid 416 former cement factory workers for 19 months, and had not compensated people whose houses were destroyed when the factory was built. The Board's Rabi Shankar Sainju said an audit showed no employee liabilities but that the Board would raise it with the Finance Ministry if the claim was genuine. Local groups stopped the depot works from August 2018 to January 2019, and the Bank told the government it would make no disbursement against the component until community grievances were addressed and the grievance process documented. A two-tier grievance mechanism was then set up, with a committee at the site and one at the ministry.
outcome: The Inspection Panel registered the request on 27 May 2020. After visiting the site and meeting the requesters, the Panel found no sufficient grounds to investigate the complaint, and recommended that consultations with local communities be strengthened in future projects. The Bank told the Panel that several of the complaints concerned actions long predating its involvement, such as land claims going back to the 1960s, and that these were outside the policy's scope. The Bank also said the project recognised the Newars as indigenous peoples and that the policy did not require a separate Indigenous Peoples Plan. Disbursements for the dry port resumed in February 2020. The project closed on 30 November 2021. The requesters say their demand for the return of the land has not been acted on.

place: Kabeli corridor 132 kV transmission line, Jhapa, Ilam and Panchthar districts, eastern Nepal

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Kabeli Transmission Project, project number P112893, credit IDA-49320 and grant IDA-H6760, approved 10 May 2011, effective 21 September 2011, closing extended by 18 months from 30 June 2015 to 31 December 2016. Component 1, at US$31.56 million, paid for a 90 km 132 kV double circuit transmission line and three new 132/33 kV substations in the Godak, Phidim and Amarpur areas; the completion report records that the fourth substation on the project, at Damak, was financed by the utility from its own resources. The completion report of 12 September 2018 rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and risk to development outcome High; the Independent Evaluation Group concurs on the outcome, rating it Moderately Unsatisfactory (ICR Review, 14 January 2019). The Evaluation Group's review says social safeguards were only partially implemented and that 55 per cent of compensation for project-affected families was paid.

companies.name: Nepal Electricity Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report. The state-owned utility that generates, transmits and distributes electricity in Nepal; it acquired the land and pays the compensation, and the report says preparation of its resettlement action plan was delayed and the issue was raised repeatedly with its management. Its Deputy Managing Director was handling the two unpaid categories. The Alternative Energy Promotion Centre implemented the rural energy component. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

community: The line runs for 90 km through hill districts of eastern Nepal and needed tower pads, a right of way and the removal of structures. About twenty months after the project closed, the completion report of September 2018 printed the state of the payments, under a heading saying there had been good progress in compensation payment since the closing. For tower pads, 188 of 228 affected families had been paid, 82 per cent; the gaps are owners with no legal title, families unable to produce legal documents, and families unwilling to accept the compensation. For structures, 41 of 82 families had been paid, 50 per cent; three families received only half because they had not yet demolished their structures, one was not paid because the landowner was absent, and 37 structures had only recently been identified and were still being valued. For the right-of-way easement fee, 673 of 1,339 affected families had been paid, 50 per cent; the gaps are difficulty identifying owners and users because the district land survey offices have no record, payments left uncollected because the amount is too small to bother with, and absentees. Resettlement and rehabilitation assistance to the owners of residential structures had still not been paid, which the report attributes to a change in senior management, and assistance to people without title had not been paid because the chief district officer was unwilling to carry out the valuation. A community school in the right of way was being rebuilt, with completion expected by the end of December 2018. Land acquisition was still going on at the closing date for the sections still under construction, and the report says the acquisition was held back mainly by delay in agreeing the compensation amount. Dissatisfaction persisted among the communities and households whose land was affected, and persistent local protest forced the line to be re-routed around about 3.8 km of the peri-urban edge of Jorsal in Phidim right at the end of the project; the report says there is no community resistance there now. The report adds that the Bank observed good progress in implementing the safeguard activities, that it has found the utility's safeguard performance satisfactory so far, and that the utility has committed in writing to finish the measures during construction.
outcome: Only the 34.5 km first section, Damak to Godak, was physically complete when the project closed on 31 December 2016; the substations stood finished but uncommissioned for a long time because no line was there to carry power to them. An external monitor was hired to follow the resettlement plan. As of August 2018, 55 per cent of the compensation due to project-affected families had been paid. The Kathmandu Post reported in October 2019 that the Kabeli corridor had finally assumed full shape in August, after twelve years.

title: Homes and shops affected by road widening and landslides on the Narayanghat-Mugling road
place: Narayanghat-Mugling road, Chitwan and Tanahun districts, Nepal

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Nepal-India Regional Trade and Transport Project, project number P144335, credit IDA-52730 and grant IDA-H8630, approved 28 June 2013, effective 10 September 2013, closed 30 November 2021. US$99.0 million committed, US$70.5 million disbursed (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 June 2022, Financing and Key Dates tables). Component 1 upgraded and expanded the 33 km Narayanghat-Mugling section of the Birgunj-Kathmandu corridor to Asian Highway standard and built four bridges. The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group concurs on the outcome and rates Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory (ICR Review, 14 September 2022, section 11).

companies.name: Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, Government of Nepal
companies.role: One of two implementing agencies named in the completion report. Its Department of Roads ran the Narayanghat-Mugling works through a project office at Mugling headed by a first-class engineer. No construction contractor is named; the report says three large works contracts were executed for the road.

community: Upgrading the 33 km road affected 131 private structures, both residential and commercial, belonging to 103 households. The completion report attributes the impacts to the road upgrade works and to landslides, and says the resettlement action plan of 2013 was updated three times, in 2014, 2016 and 2017, to deal with landslide impacts during construction. The outcome is larger than the plan: the Independent Evaluation Group records that 80 structures and 74 households were estimated at appraisal. Twenty community structures, mostly public toilets and passenger sheds, were also hit, and all twenty were rebuilt. Cash compensation, a displacement allowance, a rental stipend and a business disturbance allowance were paid to the affected households in line with the plan, except for one absentee household. Affected people also received an economic rehabilitation grant and income restoration training. A vulnerable community development plan covered project impacts on 91 households, mostly Dalit people and other minority ethnic groups.
outcome: The project closed on 30 November 2021 with most of the road improvements finished by mid-2018. Slope works at km 17 and km 26 were not completed within the project period because of the covid-19 pandemic. One affected household remained uncompensated because its owner was absent.

title: Land taken for earthquake road rebuilding, with a quarter of the compensation never reaching owners
place: Jhelum Valley Road, Muzaffarabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and National Highways N-15 and N-35 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: First Additional Financing to the Highways Rehabilitation Project, project number P099040, a US$100.0 million loan (Ln. 7341-PK) approved on 1 December 2005, after the 8 October 2005 earthquake, to reconstruct about 44 km of National Highway N-15 (the Kaghan Valley Road), rehabilitate about 25 km of National Highway N-35 (the Karakoram Highway) and rehabilitate about 59 km of the Jhelum Valley Road in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and to pay for relocation of utilities, resettlement and land acquisition (Implementation Completion and Results Report, report no. ICR2723, 21 November 2013, section 1.6.1 and section 1.7.1(a)). The loan was one of four financings of a single operation carried under the parent project number P010556, which closed on 30 June 2013. That completion report rates the project's social safeguards Moderately Satisfactory (section 2.4.2) and its overall outcome Satisfactory; the Bank's Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, because efficiency was modest given significant cost overruns (ICR Review, 11 June 2014). The completion report says the Bank financed the land acquisition itself (Annex 7, p. 49).

companies.name: National Highway Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency. A federal body under Pakistan's Ministry of Communications that owns and manages the national highway network; its Project Management Unit ran the works, and its Deputy Project Coordinators kept the complaints register. The completion report's borrower section says land acquisition was held up by delay in releasing funds by the Authority, even though the Bank was paying for the land (Annex 7, p. 49). No construction contractor is named in the documents.

companies.name: Land Revenue Departments of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Azad Jammu and Kashmir
companies.role: Provincial and state revenue offices that assessed and paid out the compensation. The unpaid balance sat in their escrow accounts at project close. The completion report also records non-posting of required staff and a lukewarm response by the provincial revenue departments, and the destruction of revenue records in the earthquake.

community: Rebuilding the three earthquake-damaged highways to national standards needed land. The completion report records about 1,007 kanals acquired for the Earthquake Damaged Roads component, valued at about Rs 108 million (US$1.1 million). Of that, Rs 76.5 million (US$0.78 million), 72 per cent, was paid to project-affected people. The remaining Rs 31 million (US$0.32 million) was not paid. The report gives four reasons: some owners died in the earthquake; some left the disaster areas for other parts of the country and could not be traced; some claims are disputed in court; and some are shamlat cases, land with many joint owners whose individual entitlements come to less than US$100 and who are unwilling to open a bank account to receive them. The report says the court cases are unlikely to be resolved in the near future, and that the money is already deposited and held in escrow accounts with the Land Revenue Departments, so compensation will eventually be paid when the cases settle. The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group adds that the project team put the disputed claims at US$0.11 million, 36 per cent of the unpaid balance. The completion report's borrower section records that the Azad Jammu and Kashmir government used land acquisition funds for other purposes rather than disbursing them to affected people, and that the land acquisition was delayed, in the borrower's words, beyond proportion to the extent of risking the suspension of disbursement. At appraisal in 2003, before the earthquake component was added, the project expected to take 6 hectares of land and affect about 350 people. On the main N-5 corridor the works stayed inside the existing right of way apart from five acres at Mitiari bypass, bought by private negotiation at market rates.
outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2013. About Rs 31 million of compensation was still unpaid, held in escrow by the revenue departments of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Azad Jammu and Kashmir, with the court cases behind part of it expected to take years. No later document showing the money paid out was found.
