title: Sixteen Per Cent of the Residents Owed Right-of-Way Payments Were Still Unpaid When Peru’s Rural Electrification Loan Closed
place: Rural sub-project areas of the Electrocentro and Hidrandina distribution companies, Peru; no document found names the places where the right-of-way payments were owed

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Rural Electrification Project (P090116, filed with the Global Environment Facility grant as P090110), Loan 7366-PE, fifty million dollars, loan agreement with the Republic of Peru dated 19 July 2006, together with Global Environment Facility Trust Fund Grant 056023-PE, which was cancelled in September 2012 after the government chose auctions for renewable electricity instead of the Small Hydro Financing Facility the grant was to finance. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 30 June 2017 gives the count: "The project triggered four of the World Bank's safeguard policies: OP/BP 4.01 on Environmental Assessment; OP/BP 4.12 on Involuntary Resettlement; OP/BP 4.10 on Indigenous Peoples; and OP/BP4.37 on Safety of Dams", the dam policy becoming not applicable when the small hydro component was cancelled. The completion report of 26 December 2013 lists the same four and gives the indigenous peoples policy as "OP 4.20 being revised as OP4.10". The three documents rate the project differently and each must be read from itself: the completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the global environment outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory; the evaluation review of 17 June 2015 rates the outcome Satisfactory; the assessment report of 30 June 2017 rates the development outcome satisfactory and the risk to it negligible. The loan's closing date was extended by eighteen months in two steps, and the assessment report says the second extension was needed "to enable right-of-way payments before project closing".

companies.name: Electrocentro
companies.role: One of the four regional distribution companies in the state holding company Distriluz, named in the appraisal document of 7 February 2006 alongside Electronorte, Hidrandina and Electronoreste. The completion report and the assessment report both name it as one of two companies that fell behind in making right-of-way payments to residents.

companies.name: Hidrandina
companies.role: Another of the four Distriluz regional distribution companies. The completion report and the assessment report both name it as the other company that fell behind in making right-of-way payments. The completion report gives its economic rate of return for the grid extension component as a negative value, the lowest of the companies it lists.

companies.name: Dirección General de Electrificación Rural, Ministerio de Energía y Minas
companies.role: The rural electrification directorate inside Peru's energy and mines ministry, which signed the subsidy agreements with the distribution companies, prepared the procurement plan and supervised contracting, and which reported the state of the right-of-way payments after the project closed. Its Directorate of Competitive Funding ran the sub-project side.

community:
The documents on this loan record two kinds of loss to people in the way of the rural power lines.

Two families were moved. The completion report of 26 December 2013 says that on involuntary resettlement "two cases of families being moved were reported and reviewed" and that the Bank's specialist concluded they had been handled in a satisfactory way. The assessment report of 30 June 2017 repeats it.

More people were owed money for rights of way across their land and had not been paid when the loan closed. The subsidy agreements made the distribution companies responsible for meeting the safeguard requirements. The assessment report says two of the nine companies, Electrocentro and Hidrandina, fell behind. Both the completion report and the assessment report give the position afterwards. The completion report: "DFC-DGER reported that 86 percent of the amount of the right of way payments corresponding to 84 percent of the affected people had been made by July 31, 2013." The assessment report: "By July 31, 2013 (one month after the closing date), DFC-DGER reported that 86 percent of the amount of right-or-way payments, which corresponded to 84 percent of the concerned residents, had been made." So 16 per cent of the residents owed money had not received it a month after the loan closed.

The assessment report sets out why. The contracts with the installation companies did not say clearly who was responsible for the payments or how they were to be arranged. It adds three further obstacles: the absence of land titles, difficulty in locating landowners, and those owners' view that the amount they were owed was not worth the time and expense of cashing it. The completion report attributes the problem in part to the involuntary resettlement framework giving inadequate emphasis to right-of-way payments. It also records the lesson drawn, that right-of-way payments and compensation for the negative impacts of construction should be inside the project cost and written into the contractors' activities.
outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2013, having been due to close on 31 December 2011. A month after closing the rural electrification directorate reported that 86 per cent of the money owed for rights of way, covering 84 per cent of the residents concerned, had been paid; the completion report and the assessment report both carry that report. The evaluation review of 17 June 2015 says the problems were resolved soon after closure. No document found says when or whether the rest was paid.

title: 23 households moved off two Manila sewerage sites, one group paid 60 days' wages to go
place: Barangay Guitnang Bayan II, San Mateo, Rizal, and the Road 5 communal septic tank compound in Barangay Project 6, Quezon City, Philippines

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P079661, Manila Third Sewerage Project, loan IBRD-73110 of Japanese yen 6,592 million, the equivalent of US$64 million, to the Land Bank of the Philippines with the guarantee of the Republic of the Philippines. The loan agreement for loan 7311-PH was conformed on 22 July 2005. The completion report of 28 December 2012, whose own data sheet gives the report date as 27 December 2012, gives approval on 21 June 2005, effectiveness on 6 March 2006, a mid-term review on 10 March 2008, an original closing date of 30 June 2010 and actual closing on 30 June 2012, with restructurings on 25 June 2010 and 17 January 2011; US$40.56 million of the US$64 million was disbursed. Environmental category A. The report says the environmental assessment policy OP 4.01 and the involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 were triggered; the Evaluation Group's review cites page 17 of the appraisal document for the same two. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Moderate. The Evaluation Group's review, posted 12 March 2015 per its own Date Posted line, rates the outcome Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and the quality of the completion report Unsatisfactory, and agrees only on risk. Among its reasons it gives that only one quarter of the planned treatment plants were operating at closure and that measured pollutant removal reached 1,415 tonnes a year against a target of 20,400.

companies.name: Manila Water Company, Inc.
companies.role: Concessionaire for the east zone of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System, implementing agency for the project and the buyer of the San Mateo site; it wrote both resettlement plans and paid the households.

companies.name: Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System
companies.role: The state corporation that owns the Metro Manila water and sewerage assets and holds the concessions. It owned the Road 5 land, terminated the lease of one occupant in April 2008 for unpaid rent and because the project needed the land, and ran the relocation there.

companies.name: Land Bank of the Philippines
companies.role: Borrower of the Bank loan and, with the concessionaire, an implementing agency; a state-owned bank whose mandate is lending to farmers and fisherfolk.

community: Eight sites were built on and two of them had people living on them. The Bank's completion report says in its social safeguards annex: "Two of the eight sub-project sites had occupants who were requested to relocate prior to land negotiations and project implementation." At the North Septage Treatment Plant site in Barangay Guitnang Bayan II, San Mateo, Rizal, there were "eleven (11) households (46 persons) ... who were allowed by the former owner to reside in the property"; when he sold it they were asked to go, and the concessionaire "prepared an ARAP and provided relocation assistance to all the displaced households." The plan of 4 March 2005 names them one by one; the heads of the families were former employees of the previous owner and the first on the list, a widow who sold at the public market and kept backyard pigs, had lived there since 1975. They were offered either housing on 24 hectares of the former owner's land in Montalban or a package of 18,000 pesos a family, which the law set at 60 days of the minimum daily wage of 285 pesos, or 17,100 pesos, plus payment for their houses at replacement cost, free transport and the right to take their building materials. The plan says they chose the second option because the money could start a small livelihood, and that some meant to go back to their home provinces in Luzon and the Visayas. It also records that they were consulted before the sale was negotiated in February 2005 and “have agreed that they will vacate the premises once the lot is sold”, puts their average household income at 15,000 pesos a month, and counts four of the eleven households as having arrived in January 2005, a month before its census. It budgeted 198,000 pesos in assistance and 33,000 pesos in transport, and says the families would get at least 60 days' notice before demolition. At the second site, the Road 5 communal septic tank in Barangay Project 6, Quezon City, the completion report says there were 12 households on land owned by the sewerage system, that they "were considered non-poor", and that "they were issued notifications to vacate the property." The relocation was run by the sewerage system with an inter-agency committee that included the Presidential Commission for the Urban Poor and the Commission on Human Rights, and each displaced household was given the standard package of 22,500 pesos, which the report describes as 60 days of the daily minimum wage, plus free hauling of their belongings. The plan written for that site in March 2005 counted three families, not twelve, headed by a former employee of the sewerage system who had been there since 1983, his unemployed cousin there since 1987, and a tricycle driver, unrelated to them, there since 1986; it said their houses sat on top of the septic tanks, that this was a risk to them, that an authority to demolish would be sought from the mayor’s office, and that they had been told in October 2003 of the need to evacuate. The same plan says of those three that they “have expressed their preference for relocation” and that the result of the first dialogues was “positive with the affected families willing to relocate after due assistance”, naming the socialised-housing option rather than the cash package as the one they were willing to take. The completion report also records that all eight sites needed land, that only one private lot was bought outright, and that the rest were handed over by local governments on conditions such as building parks and sports facilities and refurbishing government offices, which the Evaluation Group says may have cost more than buying land.
outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2012. The completion report rates environmental compliance Satisfactory and says environmental and social policies and procedures were complied with. The Evaluation Group's review of March 2015 rates the project's outcome Unsatisfactory and says the concessionaire "demonstrated lack of realism, during both preparation and implementation, regarding its ability to resolve land acquisition and community resistance issues in a timely manner (or even, in some cases, at all)", that some local governments never delivered land they had promised, and that several planned plants were dropped. Neither document says where the 23 households went or what became of them.
